curtail.n: Formal and slightly stiff, curtail usually takes an object such as spending, freedom, powers or a visit, and the idea is cutting something short or restricting it, often by authority. Stress falls on the second syllable: cur-TAIL. It is stronger than reduce because it suggests a deliberate limit, and it often appears in news, law and business writing. Collocations include curtail activities, curtail the right to, and drastically curtail. Do not confuse it with cut off, which is more complete, or with cure. In everyday talk, people say cut back on instead.
x: The council voted to curtail late-night opening hours after neighbours complained about the noise.
Heavy snow forced the airline to curtail its weekend schedule to a handful of flights.

decarbonise.n: British spelling prevails here; American writers normally write decarbonize, and both belong to the same family as carbon-neutral and net zero. The verb needs an object such as a sector, an economy or a supply chain, and it commonly appears in policy discussion and corporate reports. Stress is on the second syllable: de-CAR-bon-ise. The noun is decarbonisation. It means cutting carbon emissions, not removing carbon from a material, so avoid using it for ordinary cleaning or chemistry. It sounds technical, so in casual speech people prefer cut emissions.
x: The steel industry hopes to decarbonise its furnaces by switching from coal to hydrogen.
Several cities have pledged to decarbonise public transport before the end of the decade.

exacerbate.n: Only negative things get exacerbated: pain, tension, poverty, shortages, a crisis. You would never exacerbate something pleasant, which is the main difference from improve or increase. It is formal and common in news and academic writing, usually with the pattern exacerbate a problem or be exacerbated by something. Stress falls on the second syllable, ig-ZAS-er-bayt, and the z sound in the middle surprises learners. Aggravate is a close synonym, though aggravate also describes annoying people, which exacerbate cannot do. Another trap is mixing it up with exasperate, meaning to annoy.
x: Skipping meals will only exacerbate your headaches, so try to eat something small every few hours.
Rising rents have exacerbated the shortage of nurses in the capital.

purportedly.n: Writers use purportedly to distance themselves from a claim they cannot confirm, so it signals doubt, much like allegedly or supposedly. It sits before a participle or verb, as in purportedly stolen or purportedly written by, and it is common in journalism and legal reporting. Stress the second syllable: pur-POR-ted-ly. The adjective is purported and the verb purport; the latter is formal and often followed by to, as in a document that purports to be genuine. Avoid it for facts you know are true, because it quietly questions the information.
x: The museum bought a painting purportedly made by a famous Dutch master, only to learn it was a copy.
A video purportedly filmed last week turned out to be several years old.

underpin.n: Underpin works like a verb for foundations: you underpin a wall, but you also underpin arguments, theories, economies and policies. It takes an object, and the passive underpinned by is very frequent. Formal and academic in tone, it is close to support or form the basis of, yet it stresses what lies hidden beneath. Pronounce it with stress on the last syllable in the base form: un-der-PIN. Its past form underpinned follows the pattern of pin, pinned, with a doubled n. Do not confuse it with undermine, which means the opposite, weakening something.
x: Trust between neighbours underpins the whole system of shared gardens in the village.
Decades of careful experiments underpin the doctor's recommendation.

analogous.n: Analogous is almost always followed by to, and it describes things that are comparable in a useful way even though they differ, as in the brain being analogous to a computer. It is formal and common in science, law and essays. Stress falls on the second syllable: a-NAL-o-gus, with a hard g sound. The noun is analogy, and a-NAL-o-jee has a soft g, which trips up many learners. Similar is less technical; analogous implies a point-by-point comparison. Do not use it simply to mean the same, because analogous things are never identical.
x: Learning to ride a bicycle is analogous to learning to swim, because balance matters in both.
The court treated the new dispute as analogous to a case decided in 1998.

extraterrestrial.n: Long and technical, extraterrestrial is used for anything beyond Earth, whether life, objects or signals, and it appears in science, fiction and news. As a noun it means an alien and is often shortened to ET in casual speech. Stress is on the fourth syllable in most speakers' pronunciation: ek-stra-ter-RES-tree-al, though the main stress can shift slightly. Alien is the everyday word, while extraterrestrial sounds scientific. Do not confuse it with terrestrial, which means related to land or to Earth, the opposite meaning. A hyphen is not normally used when you write it.
x: A radio telescope picked up a strange signal that some people claimed was extraterrestrial.
Few astronomers expect to find extraterrestrial animals, but microbes on Mars remain a real possibility.

likewise.n: Likewise is a sentence-linking adverb that means in the same way, and it works in two main settings. In formal writing it joins ideas, usually after a semicolon or full stop, with a comma following. In speech it is a quick polite reply: if someone says nice to meet you, you can answer likewise. It is also used before a verb, as in watch what she does and do likewise. Also is not the same, since likewise needs a similar action or attitude. Stress falls on LIKE: LIKE-wise. Moreover and furthermore add a new point instead.
x: Our neighbours recycle all their glass; we do likewise and take it to the bottle bank every Saturday.
When the head teacher stood to applaud the choir, the audience did likewise.

accessory.n: Accessory has two key meanings. In shopping it is an extra that goes with a main item, such as phone cases, belts or scarves, and it is usually plural. In law, an accessory to a crime is someone who helps without being the main offender, and the pattern is accessory to. Stress falls on the second syllable: ak-SES-uh-ree. Spelling trap: it has a double c and a double s. It is countable, so say one accessory or several accessories. Accessories in a car or a computer shop are optional extras, unlike parts, which are essential.
x: She wore a plain black dress and added a bright silk scarf as her only accessory.
The police charged the driver as an accessory to the robbery, even though he never entered the bank.

accurately.n: Accurately is the adverb of accurate, and it describes how well a statement, measurement or action matches the facts. It typically follows or precedes verbs such as measure, predict, describe, report or reflect. Stress falls on the first syllable: AK-yer-it-lee. It is slightly stronger than correctly because it implies fine detail, not just absence of error. Do not confuse it with precisely, which stresses exact detail, or with exactly, which often answers a question. In business emails you will see please record the figures accurately, and in science it appears in the context of accurately predicting results.
x: The thermometer can measure body temperature accurately within a tenth of a degree.
Journalists have a duty to report events accurately, even when the facts are uncomfortable.

administer.n: Administer is a formal verb with two common uses. It can mean to manage an organisation, a fund or a system, and it can mean to give something to someone, especially medicine, a test or a punishment, as in administer a vaccine. Stress falls on the second syllable: ad-MIN-is-ter. The related noun administration is also the word for a government in American English, so the president's administration means his government. In ordinary speech, people say run or give instead. Nurses administer drugs, teachers administer exams, and trustees administer a charity or a will.
x: Only trained staff are allowed to administer painkillers to patients in this clinic.
A small committee will administer the scholarship fund and decide who receives each grant.

affirmative.n: Affirmative is formal and mostly appears in the phrase in the affirmative, which means yes. The opposite is negative, so an affirmative answer is a positive reply, and an affirmative sentence in grammar is one that is not a negative statement. In American English, affirmative action means policies that support groups who have faced discrimination. Stress falls on the second syllable: a-FUR-ma-tiv. In military and radio speech, people say affirmative simply to mean yes. Do not use it for friendly conversation, where it would sound stiff or funny.
x: The committee gave an affirmative reply, so building work will begin in March.
In an affirmative sentence we say she likes tea, but in a negative one she does not like tea.

airfare.n: Airfare is mainly American English and means the price you pay for a plane ticket; British speakers more often say air fare or just fare. It is uncountable, so you say the airfare is high, not an airfare. Typical partners are round-trip airfare, discount airfare and airfare to Paris. Do not confuse it with airline, the company, or with airport fees and taxes, which are sometimes added on top. Travel websites and business expense forms use the word often, and it is written as one word. The stress is on the first syllable: AIR-fair.
x: Airfare to Lisbon was cheaper in October, so we booked our holiday earlier than usual.
The grant will cover airfare and accommodation for all invited speakers.

alternate.n: Alternate is pronounced differently as a verb and an adjective, which is the main problem for learners. The verb ends with a long ay sound, AWL-ter-nayt, and means to take turns, while the adjective ends with a weak vowel, AWL-ter-nit. In American English, alternate as an adjective can mean another option, as in an alternate route, while British English prefers alternative for that. In both varieties, alternate days means every second day. Do not mix it up with alternative, which means a different choice. Alternate also takes the preposition between or with when describing a pattern.
x: The two sisters alternate weeks looking after their grandmother, so each of them gets a break.
We water the garden on alternate evenings to save as much water as possible.

alternatively.n: Alternatively introduces another option or suggestion, most often at the start of a sentence, followed by a comma. It sits in a similar place to or or on the other hand, but it is more polite and written. Typical phrases include or alternatively in emails and instructions, such as you can call us; alternatively, send an email. Do not use it where the second idea contradicts the first, because then however is better. Stress falls on the second syllable: awl-TUR-na-tiv-lee. Remember to use an adverb here, since alternative cannot replace it.
x: You could take the train, or alternatively ask a friend to give you a lift to the airport.
Customers can return the shoes in the shop. Alternatively, they can post them back free of charge.

applicable.n: Applicable is a formal adjective that says a rule, price or instruction is relevant to a person or situation. It usually appears with to, and the phrase where applicable is very common on forms, meaning only fill this in if it matters for you. The opposite is not applicable, often shortened to N/A. The stress is on the first or second syllable, and both AP-li-ka-bl and a-PLIK-a-bl are heard, with the first more common. It differs from available, which is about being obtainable. A law is applicable to citizens, but a discount is valid or available.
x: Please list your previous employers, where applicable, and attach reference letters.
The new safety rules are applicable to every worker on the building site.

appreciation.n: Appreciation covers three main ideas: gratitude, understanding of quality, and an increase in value. It is uncountable in the first two senses, as in show appreciation or an appreciation of music, and the phrase in appreciation of leads to a reason for thanks. In finance, the appreciation of a currency means it becomes stronger, the opposite of depreciation. The stress falls on the third syllable: a-pree-shee-AY-shun. It is more formal and warmer than thanks. A speech might include words of appreciation, and a teacher might hope for greater appreciation of poetry.
x: The team gave the retiring manager a card to express their appreciation for twenty years of help.
A deeper appreciation of local history makes a walk through the old town much more interesting.

attire.n: Attire is a formal word for clothes, usually clothes suited to an event, and it is uncountable. It appears in invitations and dress codes: formal attire, smart casual attire, business attire. Clothing is the neutral word, and clothes is the everyday one, whereas attire carries an official tone. Stress falls on the second syllable: a-TIRE. The verb is rare today, found mostly in the passive, as in attired in black. Do not use it for a single item, since you cannot say an attire. Wedding invitations may specify beach attire, which simply means light clothing suitable for the sand.
x: The invitation states that evening attire is required for the charity dinner.
Visitors in casual attire were politely asked to change before entering the restaurant.

attorney.n: Attorney is the standard American word for a lawyer who can act for clients, and it is rare in British English, where solicitor and barrister are used. Typical combinations are district attorney, defence attorney or attorney general. In the United States, a power of attorney lets you authorise someone else to handle legal and financial matters, and that phrase is used in the UK too. Stress falls on the second syllable: a-TUR-nee. Do not confuse the legal title with someone simply representing you at work. Attorney at law is a formal, slightly old-fashioned alternative.
x: After the accident, she hired an attorney to deal with the insurance company.
The district attorney announced that no charges would be brought against the driver.

automotive.n: Automotive is an adjective that relates to motor vehicles, and it mainly appears in business phrases such as the automotive industry, automotive parts or automotive engineering. It is formal and technical and is seldom used in everyday talk, where people say car instead. Stress falls on the third syllable: aw-toh-MOH-tiv. Do not confuse it with automatic, which means working by itself, or with automobile, the noun that the American press uses for car. As a rule it comes before a noun, and you would not say my brother is automotive.
x: Many engineers in this region work for automotive suppliers that build gearboxes and brakes.
The automotive sector has been slowed by a worldwide shortage of computer chips.

availability.n: Availability is an uncountable noun meaning whether something can be obtained, booked or used, and it is a staple of shopping and booking language. Common patterns include check availability, subject to availability, limited availability and room availability. It can also describe a person's free time, as in please send me your availability for next week. Stress falls on the third syllable: a-vay-la-BIL-i-tee. The adjective available is far more common, and many learners wrongly write avaiability by dropping a letter. It does not mean the same as accessibility, which is about how easy something is to reach or use.
x: Please check ticket availability before you travel, because the museum sometimes sells out.
Our availability is limited in August, as most of the staff are on holiday.

bankruptcy.n: Bankruptcy is the legal state of being unable to pay your debts, and it applies to individuals and firms. Common verbs are file for, declare, go into and avoid bankruptcy, and the adjective is bankrupt, with the verb to go bankrupt. It is uncountable in general use, although a countable use appears in reports such as the number of bankruptcies. Stress falls on the first syllable: BANK-rupt-see. The pronunciation includes a p that some people drop. It is stronger than insolvency in everyday news, and it differs from liquidation, which is the process of selling assets afterwards.
x: The family business collapsed under heavy debts and finally went into bankruptcy last spring.
Mounting medical bills pushed thousands of households toward bankruptcy, the study found.

biography.n: Biography is a book or text about someone's life, written by another person; if you write it about yourself, it is an autobiography. A short professional version on a website or conference programme is also called a bio, which is informal. Stress falls on the second syllable: by-OG-ra-fee. The word is countable: a biography, two biographies. Typical verbs are write, publish and read a biography. The adjective is biographical, as in biographical details. Do not confuse the writer, called a biographer, with the subject. Memoir is a related term that focuses on a particular period of the author's own life.
x: I borrowed a biography of Marie Curie from the library and finished it in a weekend.
The speaker's biography in the programme listed her awards but not her early career.

boardroom.n: Boardroom is a closed noun for the room where a company's directors meet, and it also stands for top-level management and its decisions. In phrases like boardroom battle or boardroom politics, the word suggests power struggles among senior people. Stress falls on the first syllable: BORD-room. It is written as one word in most modern texts. The words meeting room and conference room are neutral, ordinary options, but boardroom has a more serious and prestigious tone. In British English the term is the same, and a table in a boardroom is typically long and polished.
x: The chairman called an urgent meeting in the boardroom to discuss the falling sales figures.
A bitter boardroom dispute over the firm's future ended with two directors resigning.

cartridge.n: Cartridge is a sealed container that you insert into a machine, most often an ink or toner cartridge for a printer. It also names a case containing a bullet, and in gaming it was the removable unit holding a video game. The pronunciation is KAR-trij, with a soft final sound, and the spelling includes an unexpected d, which causes common mistakes. It is countable. Phrases include replace the cartridge, refill a cartridge and empty cartridge. Do not mix it up with a capsule or pod, which refers to coffee machine containers.
x: The printer stopped working because the black ink cartridge was completely empty.
Pull out the old cartridge gently and push the new one in until it clicks.

collector.n: Collector is the person who gathers things, either for a hobby, such as stamps, coins or art, or as part of a job, such as a ticket collector or a tax collector. In British English a bin collector is a refuse worker. The noun comes from the verb collect, and stress falls on the second syllable: kuh-LEK-ter. Typical partners are art collector, private collector and rubbish collector. A collector differs from a hoarder, who keeps things without selection, and the word is more neutral than enthusiast. Rare items can be called collector's items.
x: A private collector paid a record price for the old map at the auction.
The collector at the station checks every passenger's ticket before the train leaves.

commonly.n: Commonly means often or in most cases, and it normally goes before a past participle or verb: commonly used, commonly known as, commonly found. It also suggests wide recognition, so it works well when introducing a nickname or alternative name. Stress falls on the first syllable: KOM-un-lee. It differs from usually, which describes habits, and from generally, which sounds like a rule with exceptions. Do not use it for people in the sense of being rude, a meaning that belongs to the adjective common. Scientific texts say commonly misunderstood or commonly reported.
x: The disease is commonly spread through contaminated water in areas without proper sanitation.
Rosemary, commonly grown in pots, will survive the winter in mild regions.

complimentary.n: Complimentary means given free, usually by a business to be polite, as in a complimentary drink, coffee or upgrade. It has a second meaning of expressing praise, as in complimentary remarks. The spelling is the tricky part: complimentary with an i relates to compliments, while complementary with an e means completing or matching something else. Stress falls on the third syllable: kom-pli-MEN-ta-ree. Hotels and airlines use the word often. Free is more everyday, and on the house is a spoken expression used at restaurants and bars.
x: Every guest receives a complimentary bottle of water and a map of the city at check-in.
Her speech was extremely complimentary about the volunteers who ran the event.

comprehension.n: Comprehension means the ability to understand, especially language, and it is uncountable. In exams, reading comprehension and listening comprehension are standard sections. Stress falls on the third syllable: kom-pre-HEN-shun. It appears in the fixed phrase beyond comprehension, meaning too hard or strange to understand. Understanding is the ordinary word, while comprehension is more formal or educational. Do not confuse it with comprehensive, which means complete and covering everything. The related verb is comprehend, which is rare in speech and used mostly in writing or for abstract ideas.
x: Her comprehension of spoken French improved quickly once she moved to Lyon.
The horror of the event was almost beyond comprehension for the crowd.

consecutive.n: Consecutive describes things that follow each other in order with no break, such as consecutive days, wins or numbers. It stresses the unbroken line, which separates it from successive, a close but slightly more formal synonym that allows small gaps. Stress falls on the second syllable: kun-SEK-yoo-tiv. It is most often used before a noun and with a number: the third consecutive year. Do not confuse it with consequent or with continuous, which describes something that never stops. Weather reports and sports results are typical places to meet it, for instance five consecutive wet weekends.
x: The striker has scored in six consecutive matches, which is a new record for the club.
It rained for four consecutive days, and the river finally burst its banks.

correspondence.n: Correspondence is an uncountable noun for letters, emails or messages exchanged, and it also means a similarity or link between two things. In offices it appears in phrases like business correspondence, handle the correspondence and further correspondence. It takes a singular verb. Stress falls on the third syllable: kor-uh-SPON-dens, and the spelling has double r and double e issues for learners. The related verb correspond means both to write to someone and to match, followed by with. A correspondent can be a journalist abroad or a regular letter writer, so context matters.
x: All correspondence about the contract should be sent to the legal department by post or email.
The archive holds decades of private correspondence between the two scientists.

cosmetic.n: Cosmetic works in two ways. As an adjective it relates to products or procedures that improve appearance, as in cosmetic surgery, and it can also describe changes that are superficial and do not solve the real problem, which is a slightly critical use. As a noun it usually appears in the plural, cosmetics, meaning make-up. Stress falls on the second syllable: koz-MET-ik. Do not confuse it with comestic, which does not exist. Beauty is a broader word, and cosmetic repairs on a car mean fixing only how it looks, not how it runs.
x: The company has promised only cosmetic changes to its website, not a full redesign.
She works for a firm that tests cosmetic products without using animals.

counselor.n: Counselor is the American spelling; British English writes counsellor, with a double l. It means someone trained to give advice and emotional support, in schools, careers, therapy and also at summer camps. Typical combinations are school counselor, career counselor and grief counselor. Stress falls on the first syllable: KOWN-sel-er. Do not confuse it with councillor, an elected member of a local council, which sounds almost the same. A counselor gives guidance for personal problems, while a consultant gives specialist business advice, and a lawyer is sometimes addressed as counsel in court.
x: The school counselor met with each student to talk about subjects for the next year.
After the accident, he saw a counselor once a week to help him cope with the stress.

courier.n: Courier can mean a person or company that carries packages and urgent documents, and it can also mean a guide who looks after a tour group, mainly in British English. Stress falls on the first syllable in the delivery sense, KUR-ee-er, though the pronunciation KOOR-ee-er also exists. Phrases include send by courier, courier service and motorcycle courier. It is not identical to post, as couriers promise speed and tracking. In writing, use by courier without an article. Delivery driver is a more casual term, particularly for food and online shopping.
x: We sent the signed contract by courier so that it would arrive before the deadline.
A cycle courier weaved through the traffic with a package strapped to his back.

courtesy.n: Courtesy is polite behaviour, and it has an extra business meaning of something provided free as a favour. In phrases like courtesy of, it credits who supplied something, such as a photo. A courtesy call is a friendly call made to inform rather than to sell, and a courtesy car is one lent while yours is repaired. Stress falls on the first syllable: KUR-ti-see, and the first syllable sounds like cur. It is uncountable in the sense of good manners. Politeness is the neutral synonym, and courtesy is a bit more formal and respectful.
x: He had the courtesy to phone and warn us that he would be late for the meeting.
The garage lent me a courtesy car while my own was being repaired.

culinary.n: Culinary is an adjective for cooking and kitchen skills, and it is rarely used in casual speech. It appears before nouns, as in culinary school, culinary arts, culinary skills and culinary tradition, and it gives the topic a professional or cultural flavour. Pronunciation has two accepted variants: KUL-in-air-ee in American English and KUL-in-uh-ree in British English. Do not confuse it with cooking, which is neutral, or with gastronomic, which concerns food enjoyment and fine dining. You would not call a recipe culinary, but you can describe a trip as a culinary tour.
x: After finishing culinary school, she opened a small bakery near the harbour.
The region is famous for its culinary traditions, especially its cheeses and smoked meats.

cumulative.n: Cumulative means growing by successive additions, so the total effect becomes larger over time. It is common in finance, science and education: cumulative interest, cumulative effect, cumulative total and cumulative exam scores. Stress falls on the first syllable: KYOO-myoo-la-tiv. It differs from total because it highlights the gradual process, and it differs from additional, which stresses new items. Do not confuse it with accumulate, the verb from the same family, whose stress falls on the second syllable. The adverb cumulatively exists, but it is far rarer. A cumulative mark in a course adds up every test.
x: The cumulative effect of many small mistakes eventually brought the whole project to a stop.
Her cumulative score over the three exams was enough to secure a place at university.

dealership.n: Dealership is a business, usually selling cars, that holds a licence to sell and service the products of a manufacturer. Typical combinations are car dealership, truck dealership and authorised dealership; you buy a car from or at a dealership. Stress falls on the first syllable: DEE-ler-ship. A dealership differs from a garage, which mainly repairs vehicles, and from a showroom, which is just the display room. The word also exists for a business holding rights to sell other goods, such as farm machinery or motorbikes. It is countable and chiefly used in the United States.
x: We test drove three models at the local dealership before deciding which one to buy.
The dealership offered a generous trade-in price for my old van.

decoration.n: Decoration is countable when it means an ornament, such as Christmas decorations, and uncountable when it means the act or art of making a place attractive, as in interior decoration. It also means an honour, such as a military medal. Stress falls on the third syllable: dek-o-RAY-shun. The verb is decorate, and in British English a decorator is someone who paints and wallpapers rooms. Do not confuse it with design, which is about planning. Typical phrases are party decorations, wall decorations and put up decorations. It generally suggests pretty extras rather than structure.
x: The children spent the afternoon making paper decorations for the school fair.
Painting the walls was easy; choosing the decoration for each room took far longer.

dedication.n: Dedication has two senses. It means strong commitment to a task or cause, as in dedication to teaching, and it means the short message at the front of a book, song or event honouring someone. In the first sense it is uncountable and positive, close to commitment but with more emotional weight. Stress falls on the third syllable: ded-i-KAY-shun. Common phrases include hard work and dedication and a dedication to someone. A plaque unveiled at a ceremony is a dedication too. Do not confuse the noun with the adjective dedicated, which describes a devoted person or a purpose-built facility.
x: Her dedication to the choir meant she never missed a rehearsal in ten years.
The author wrote a touching dedication to her grandmother at the start of the novel.

departmental.n: Departmental is an adjective meaning of or belonging to a department, and it is widespread in universities, companies and government offices. Typical phrases include departmental meeting, departmental head, departmental budget and departmental policy. Stress falls on the third syllable: dee-part-MEN-tl. It is a rather dry, administrative word and is used before a noun. It is not the same as interdepartmental, which concerns more than one department, and it differs from company-wide. In British English a department store is a large shop, but the adjective departmental is not used for shops.
x: The English department holds a departmental meeting on the first Monday of every month.
Any departmental spending above a thousand pounds needs written approval from the director.

desperate.n: Desperate describes someone in such a bad situation that they will try anything, or something done in that spirit. The usual pattern is desperate for something, desperate to do something or a desperate attempt. In informal British speech, it is also used lightly: I'm desperate for a cup of tea. Stress falls on the first syllable: DES-pur-it, which differs from the verb separate. The noun is desperation. It is stronger than eager or anxious, and a desperate measure is risky and last-minute. Do not use it for mild wishes in formal writing.
x: The villagers were desperate for clean water after the pumps failed during the drought.
In a desperate attempt to catch the train, he ran across the platform with his bags.

deteriorate.n: Deteriorate means to get steadily worse, and it is used for health, weather, relationships, buildings and conditions. It is an intransitive verb, so no object follows: the situation deteriorated, never they deteriorated the situation. Stress falls on the second syllable: de-TEER-ee-uh-rayt, and the noun deterioration has a long fifth syllable. Typical adverbs are rapidly and steadily. It is less sudden than collapse and more formal than get worse. Do not use it for something suddenly broken. Doctors and meteorologists often use the word, and it is rarely used for people in a moral sense.
x: The old bridge has deteriorated so badly that engineers have closed it to heavy trucks.
His health began to deteriorate soon after he retired, and he needed daily care.

drastically.n: Drastically is an adverb meaning in an extreme way, and it goes with verbs of change, such as reduce, change, cut, rise or fall. It always implies that the change is large and often unwelcome or shocking. Stress falls on the second syllable: DRAS-tik-lee, with the pronunciation of -ically as -ik-lee. It is stronger than significantly and more dramatic than greatly. Do not use it for tiny differences. It also fits the adjective drastic: drastic measures, drastic changes, drastic action. Policy documents, weather reports and economic news use it often, as in drastically lower prices.
x: The company drastically cut its production after demand for petrol cars fell.
Traffic in the city centre dropped drastically once the congestion charge was introduced.

duplicate.n: Duplicate is a word with a split personality in pronunciation. As a noun or adjective it ends in a short weak sound, DYOO-pli-kit, and means an exact copy, while the verb ends in a clear ay sound, DYOO-pli-kayt, meaning to make a copy or to repeat unnecessarily. A duplicate key is a spare. In computing, duplicate a file means copy it, and duplicate entries are repeated records. Copy is the everyday word, whereas duplicate stresses exactness. In work settings, the phrase in duplicate means two identical copies, as in sign the form in duplicate.
x: I made a duplicate of the front-door key and left it with a neighbour.
Please do not duplicate work that the research team has already completed.

economically.n: Economically is an adverb with two senses. It relates to the economy, as in economically weak regions or economically active people, and it also means in a way that saves money, as in a car that runs economically. Stress falls on the third syllable: ek-uh-NOM-ik-lee. Do not confuse it with economical, the adjective for thrifty or cheap to run, and with the school subject economics. It often modifies adjectives like viable, sensible or disadvantaged. In news English, it commonly points to the national or regional picture, so it is a little more formal than financially.
x: The island is economically dependent on tourism, so a poor summer hurts everyone.
The new boiler heats the whole house economically, using far less gas than the old one.

efficiently.n: Efficiently describes doing something well with little waste of time, effort or money. It usually follows verbs such as work, run, operate, use or organise, and often pairs with effectively, but the words differ: efficiently is about the amount of resources used, while effectively is about getting the intended result. You can work efficiently and still miss the goal. Stress falls on the second syllable: i-FISH-ent-lee. The adjective is efficient and the noun efficiency. Do not use it for people's feelings. Managers and engineers use it often, for instance efficiently heated homes.
x: The new warehouse layout lets staff pack and dispatch orders far more efficiently than before.
She organised the conference efficiently, and every speaker started exactly on time.

enthusiastically.n: Enthusiastically means with eager energy and interest, usually of people responding to ideas, offers or events, and it goes with verbs like greet, respond, support, applaud or join in. Stress falls on the third syllable: en-thoo-zee-AS-tik-lee. The adverb is long, so many learners hesitate over the spelling, with th after the en. It is warmer than willingly and stronger than happily. Do not mix it up with the noun enthusiasm. In reports and reviews, it implies an audience that clearly shows excitement, for example crowds cheering, and it is almost always positive.
x: The crowd clapped enthusiastically as the band walked on to the stage.
When we announced the trip, the students responded enthusiastically and signed up within an hour.

environmentally.n: Environmentally is an adverb meaning in a way concerned with or affecting the natural environment. It most often appears in the set phrase environmentally friendly, together with environmentally aware, environmentally sensitive and environmentally responsible. Stress falls on the third syllable: en-vy-ron-MEN-tl-ee. Many learners drop the n in the middle of the word when they write or say it. It is more formal than green, which is the casual term in advertising. Do not use it to describe ordinary surroundings, such as a room's atmosphere. An environmentally sensitive area is protected from building because of its wildlife.
x: The supermarket promised to use only environmentally friendly packaging within two years.
Farming methods that are environmentally responsible protect rivers as well as soil.

evacuate.n: Evacuate means to move people out of a place because of danger, and the object is normally the people or the place, so you evacuate residents or evacuate a building. People can also be evacuated, which is the common passive form: thousands were evacuated. Stress falls on the second syllable: i-VAK-yoo-ayt. It is more organised than flee, which is what people do on their own. The noun is evacuation and evacuee is a person who is moved. A medical meaning exists but is rare and technical. Typical causes are fire, flood, bombs or gas leaks.
x: Police asked residents to evacuate the neighbourhood as the wildfire moved closer.
Staff calmly evacuated the cinema when the fire alarm began to ring.

exceptional.n: Exceptional means unusually good, and sometimes just unusual, as in exceptional circumstances. The two senses can mix: exceptional talent is positive, whereas an exceptional case is simply an exception to a rule. Stress falls on the second syllable: ik-SEP-shun-al. Do not confuse it with exceptionable, a rare word meaning open to objection, or with exception, the noun. It is stronger than very good and fits references, service, quality and performance. Adverb: exceptionally. Rules at work or school often mention exceptional circumstances, which allow something that is not usually permitted.
x: Her exam results were exceptional, and she was offered a scholarship at once.
Refunds are only given in exceptional circumstances, such as serious illness.

exclusively.n: Exclusively means only and not including anyone or anything else. It goes with words such as for, to, on, available or focus, as in available exclusively to members. It is more formal than only and appears in shops, advertising and contracts. Stress falls on the second syllable: ik-SKLOO-siv-lee. Do not confuse it with excessively, which means too much, and note that exclusive can also mean expensive or elite. Placing the word matters: she works exclusively for us means no one else, whereas exclusively she works for us sounds odd. Marketing often uses it for special offers.
x: This reduced rate is offered exclusively to people who book directly on our website.
The restaurant uses locally grown vegetables exclusively, so the menu changes with the seasons.

expedite.n: Expedite is a formal business verb meaning to make a process happen faster, and it normally takes an object such as delivery, an application, an order or a payment. It is the opposite of delay. Stress falls on the first syllable: EK-spi-dyt, and the verb should not be confused with expedition, which is a journey. Typical phrases are expedite shipping, expedite the process and expedited service. It does not necessarily mean the work is done immediately, only that it moves ahead of normal speed. In everyday talk, speed up is the natural choice.
x: The office offers a paid service to expedite passport applications for urgent travellers.
A phone call from the manager helped expedite the repair of our broken heater.

expertise.n: Expertise is uncountable and means special skill or knowledge gained by training or experience. Typical partners are technical expertise, legal expertise, area of expertise and have expertise in. It is usually followed by in or on, and the phrase lack of expertise is typical in job and project discussions. Stress falls on the third syllable: ek-spur-TEEZ, and it ends in a z sound rather than s. Do not confuse it with expert, which is a person, and which can also be an adjective. Know-how is a casual relative. A team may bring in outside expertise when it lacks it.
x: The charity needs volunteers with expertise in accounting and fundraising.
Her expertise in desert ecology made her the obvious choice to lead the expedition.

explanatory.n: Explanatory describes something that is meant to explain, and it commonly sits before nouns such as note, text, leaflet, diagram or footnote. Stress falls on the second syllable: ik-SPLAN-a-tor-ee, and the first syllable is weak. It is close to self-explanatory, which means so clear that nothing needs to be explained. Do not mix them up: an explanatory note is added to make things clear, but a self-explanatory sign needs no note. It also differs from descriptive, which only shows what something is like. Textbooks, forms and legal documents often include explanatory notes.
x: The booklet includes an explanatory note on how to read the weather map.
Each chart came with a short explanatory paragraph written in plain language.

familiarity.n: Familiarity is uncountable and means good knowledge of something, or the feeling that something is well known. Typical forms are familiarity with a subject, a lack of familiarity and a sense of familiarity. In job adverts it often appears in the pattern familiarity with software, which is a weaker requirement than expertise. Stress falls on the third syllable: fuh-mil-ee-AR-i-tee. The proverb familiarity breeds contempt means people dislike what they know too well. The adjective is familiar, used with to or with, and the verb phrase is become familiar with.
x: A basic familiarity with spreadsheets is enough for this part-time office job.
There was a comforting familiarity about the little cafe, with its creaking floor and old posters.

flextime.n: Flextime is mostly American English, and in Britain the usual term is flexitime, or flexible working hours. It means a system where employees choose when to start and finish work, within limits, often around core hours when everyone must be present. The word is uncountable and normally written as one word, although flex-time also occurs. Stress falls on the first syllable: FLEKS-tyme. It differs from part-time, which reduces the number of hours, and from remote work, which concerns the place. Parents often want flextime to match school hours.
x: Our firm introduced flextime so that parents can start later after the school run.
On flextime she works from seven until three, which gives her the afternoons free.

footwear.n: Footwear is an uncountable collective noun for anything worn on the feet, such as shoes, boots, trainers and sandals. Because it is uncountable you cannot say a footwear or two footwears; you say a pair of shoes or some footwear. It is used on shop signs, safety notices and in sport and fashion, with phrases like safety footwear, outdoor footwear and the footwear industry. Stress falls on the first syllable: FOOT-wair. It is more formal than shoes. Do not use it for socks, which count as hosiery or clothing.
x: Sturdy footwear is essential for the mountain trail, as the ground is steep and rocky.
The shop sells sports clothing and footwear for runners at very fair prices.

foreman.n: Foreman is the person who supervises a team of workers, typically on a building site or in a factory, and it also names the leader of a jury in British English. Stress falls on the first syllable: FOR-man, and the two syllables sound like a single short word. The plural is foremen. Because the word contains man, many workplaces now use supervisor or site manager, though foreman is still in use, and forewoman exists as a feminine form. A foreman is below a manager and has direct contact with the workers. Typical phrases are site foreman and shop-floor foreman.
x: The foreman showed the new workers where to find the safety helmets before the shift began.
As jury foreman, he read out the verdict to the silent courtroom.

formally.n: Formally has two main meanings. It can mean in an official way, as in formally announced, formally charged or formally opened, and it can mean in a formal style, as in dress formally. Do not confuse it with formerly, which means in the past; the spelling differs by one letter, and learners swap them often. Stress falls on the first syllable: FOR-muh-lee. Before an event is formally approved, it may already be informally agreed. It is the opposite of informally. In law and politics, a formally recognised party has official status.
x: The prime minister will formally open the new hospital on Friday morning.
She was formally introduced to the board, though everyone already knew her by sight.

freighter.n: Freighter is a ship or an aircraft built to carry cargo instead of passengers. The word comes from freight, goods transported in bulk, and the noun is countable: a freighter, two freighters, with phrases like cargo freighter and ocean freighter. Stress falls on the first syllable: FRAY-ter. It is not the same as a ferry, which carries people and vehicles, or a tanker, which carries liquids. In British English, you also hear cargo ship and container ship. The word can also describe a large truck in rare, older usage. Freighters often travel on fixed routes between ports.
x: The freighter docked at dawn and cranes began lifting the containers on to the quay.
A cargo freighter carrying grain was stuck in the canal for nearly a week.

frustrate.n: Frustrate is a verb meaning to make someone feel annoyed or helpless because they cannot achieve something, and it can also mean to prevent a plan from succeeding. In the second sense it takes plans, efforts or attempts as the object: frustrate the investigation. Stress falls on the first syllable: FRUS-trayt. Learners often confuse the endings: frustrated describes how a person feels, while frustrating describes what causes the feeling. The noun is frustration. It is stronger than annoy, but milder than enrage. Delays, bureaucracy and slow internet frustrate people.
x: Bad weather frustrated our attempts to reach the summit before the afternoon storm.
It frustrates me when the website crashes just as I click the payment button.

garment.n: Garment is a formal or technical word for a single item of clothing, and it is used in fashion, textile trade and care labels. The collective expressions are the garment industry and garment workers, and it is typically countable: a garment, three garments. Stress falls on the first syllable: GAR-ment. Clothes has no singular form, so garment is helpful when you need one piece. It is more formal than item of clothing and more neutral than dress or coat. Laundry labels advise on how to wash the garment, and shops talk about outer garments.
x: Please check the label inside each garment before washing, because some fabrics shrink.
Thousands of garment workers marched to demand a higher minimum wage.

generalization.n: Generalization is a statement or idea that applies broadly based on limited examples, and it carries a slightly negative edge when it ignores exceptions: sweeping generalization, hasty generalization. In academic writing, making a careful generalization from research data is positive. British writers spell it generalisation. Stress falls on the fourth syllable: jen-ra-li-ZAY-shun. The verb is generalize, usually followed by from or about. Stereotype is a close relative, though stereotypes concern fixed images of groups, while generalization may be statistical. Avoid it in phrases like generalizations about all men, because such claims rarely hold.
x: It is a generalization to say that teenagers dislike reading, since many of them love books.
From a sample of only twenty people, the scientists could not make a reliable generalization.

hazard.n: Hazard is a danger or risk, and it appears in safety language: health hazard, fire hazard, trip hazard, and hazard lights on a car. It is countable. Stress falls on the first syllable: HAZ-erd. The adjective is hazardous, and as a verb it appears in the phrase hazard a guess, meaning to offer a guess with some risk of being wrong. Hazard is stronger than problem and more specific than risk, since a hazard is the source of potential harm, while risk is the chance that harm occurs. Loose cables on a floor are a hazard.
x: Ice on the footpath is a serious hazard for elderly people walking to the shops.
I would hazard a guess that the meeting will run past six o'clock.

hazardous.n: Hazardous is the adjective of hazard and describes things that are dangerous to health or safety. It is more formal and technical than dangerous, and typical phrases include hazardous waste, hazardous materials, hazardous chemicals and hazardous conditions. Stress falls on the first syllable: HAZ-er-dus. It can also mean risky, as in a hazardous journey. Do not mix it up with harmful, which concerns damage to health, or with hazard, the noun. Labels on containers and regulations use the term, and workers need protective clothing when handling hazardous substances. A hazardous road might be icy, narrow or steep.
x: Hazardous chemicals must be kept in a locked cupboard away from the main workshop.
Driving in thick fog on a mountain road is hazardous even for experienced drivers.

healthful.n: Healthful means good for your health and is mainly American English, which separates it from healthy, since a person is healthy but food or a habit is healthful. In practice many speakers still say healthy for both, so healthful sounds slightly formal and precise. It is common in nutrition writing: healthful diet, healthful foods, healthful lifestyle. Stress falls on the first syllable: HELTH-ful. Do not use it for people, because a healthful person sounds odd. Wholesome is another close word, suggesting simple, natural and morally good as well. Dietitians prefer the term when they describe meal choices.
x: The cafe offers healthful snacks made with fruit, nuts and seeds instead of sugar.
Walking to work every morning is a simple and healthful habit that costs nothing.

hereby.n: Hereby is a formal word used in legal and official language to show that the words themselves perform the action, as in I hereby declare the meeting closed. It typically goes before a verb such as declare, certify, confirm or resign. Stress falls on the second syllable: heer-BY. It sounds ceremonial and old-fashioned in ordinary conversation, so people use it in jokes or in formal letters and contracts. It differs from therefore, which gives a reason. The noun phrase is not needed, because hereby already means by this document or statement.
x: The mayor hereby declares the new library officially open to the public.
I hereby confirm that the information in this form is true and complete.

hesitation.n: Hesitation is a pause or reluctance before acting or speaking, usually because of doubt. It is mostly uncountable, but a countable use exists for individual pauses in speech: a brief hesitation. The best-known phrase is without hesitation, which means immediately and willingly, and it often appears in polite emails: please contact us without hesitation. Another is have no hesitation in doing something. Stress falls on the third syllable: hez-i-TAY-shun. The verb is hesitate, and there is a difference from delay, which is a longer time. A hesitation in a performance may suggest nerves.
x: Without a moment's hesitation, the lifeguard jumped into the cold water to save the boy.
There was a slight hesitation in her voice when she accepted the invitation.

homeless.n: Homeless is an adjective meaning having nowhere to live, and the phrase the homeless works as a plural noun for such people, though many writers now prefer people experiencing homelessness as more respectful. Related forms are homelessness and homeless shelter. Stress falls on the first syllable: HOME-les. In British English, it also appears in official language, as in a homeless family being given temporary housing by a council. It differs from poor, since a person may have little money yet still have a home. Charities and local governments use the word often.
x: The charity opens an extra homeless shelter in the city whenever the temperature drops below zero.
After the flood, hundreds of families were left homeless and spent weeks in tents.

illogical.n: Illogical means not based on clear reasoning, and it suggests that a conclusion or behaviour does not follow from the facts. It differs from irrational, which is closer to emotional or unreasonable, and from unreasonable, which refers to fairness. Illogical is milder and calmer, so you can politely say your argument seems illogical. Stress falls on the second syllable: i-LOJ-i-kal, with a doubled l in the spelling because the prefix il- joins logical. The noun is illogicality, which is rare. In debates, a speaker may criticise an illogical plan or an illogical sequence of events.
x: It seems illogical to buy a second car when nobody in the family drives very often.
His illogical argument fell apart when someone asked for a single piece of evidence.

inappropriate.n: Inappropriate means not suitable for a particular situation, and it is usually about behaviour, language, clothes or timing, as in inappropriate comments or inappropriate content. It is more polite than rude, which makes it a favourite word in workplaces and schools. The pattern is inappropriate for or inappropriate to something, and also inappropriate to do something. Stress falls on the third syllable: in-uh-PRO-pree-it. The opposite is appropriate, and the adverb is inappropriately. It does not necessarily mean illegal; a joke at a funeral may be inappropriate but not against the law.
x: Jeans and trainers would be inappropriate for an interview at a bank.
The headmaster warned pupils that inappropriate language would not be tolerated in the corridor.

incoming.n: Incoming describes something arriving or about to begin, and it appears before a noun: incoming calls, incoming mail, incoming flights, incoming students and the incoming president, who is about to take office. It is the opposite of outgoing, which can also mean friendly and sociable when used for people. Stress falls on the first syllable: IN-kum-ing. It is not used after a verb, so you would not say the call is incoming in formal writing, although soldiers say it in warnings. Phone systems, inboxes and airports use the word often.
x: Incoming messages are sorted automatically into folders by the email program.
The incoming manager has promised to meet every member of staff in her first week.
